extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduate/graduate students learning algebraic topology (homology, categories, functors)
extracted.subtask_description: Expository textbook material on categories, functors, natural transformations, singular homology, and classical applications (Invariance of Domain, Borsuk–Ulam, Alexander horned sphere, division algebras). Intended as learning/reference material for students of algebraic topology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a category
rubrics_metrics.description: A category consists of objects X, Y, Z ∈ Ob(C) and morphisms with identity morphisms 11 satisfying f ◦ 11 = f, 11 ◦ f = f, and composition associative: (f ◦ g) ◦ h = f ◦ (g ◦ h).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes many examples and variants: category of topological spaces (continuous maps), subcategories obtained by restricting objects (e.g., CW complexes) or morphisms (e.g., homeomorphisms); category of groups (homomorphisms), abelian groups, modules; category of sets (all functions, injections, surjections, bijections); categories where morphisms are not functions (a group as a one-object category gives a monoid when inverses are not required); a poset (X, ≤) can be a category with at most one morphism between any two objects; homotopy category uses homotopy classes of maps as morphisms (composition well-defined on homotopy classes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Category-with-one-object ⇔ monoid
rubrics_metrics.description: Any group G can be viewed as a category with one object and G as the morphisms; if only associativity and left/right identity are required (no inverses) one gets a monoid, i.e., a category with one object.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains the relationship between algebraic notions (group, monoid) and categorical viewpoint; useful when modelling algebraic structures as categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poset as a category
rubrics_metrics.description: A partially ordered set (X, ≤) can be considered a category where objects are elements of X and there is a unique morphism x→y exactly when x ≤ y; x ≤ x gives the identity morphism and transitivity gives composition; the condition x ≤ y and y ≤ x implying x = y means there is at most one morphism between any two objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to relate order-theoretic structures to categorical constructions and to view simplicial/Δ-complex constructions later (e.g., simplices as posets).

rubrics_metrics.name: Covariant functor definition
rubrics_metrics.description: A functor F from a category C to a category D assigns to each object X in C an object F(X) in D and to each morphism f ∈ Mor(X,Y) in C a morphism F(f) ∈ Mor(F(X),F(Y)) in D, such that F(11) = 11 and F(f ◦ g) = F(f) ◦ F(g).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: singular homology functor H_n (with properties 11_* = 11 and (f g)_* = f_* g_*), singular chain complex functor S(·) assigning to a space its singular complex and to a map f the induced chain map, algebraic homology functor assigning to a chain complex its sequence of homology groups and induced homomorphisms. Composition of functors (e.g., space → singular complex → simplicial chain complex → homology) yields standard constructions like singular homology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contravariant functor definition
rubrics_metrics.description: A contravariant functor assigns to f ∈ Mor(X,Y) a morphism F(f) ∈ Mor(F(Y),F(X)) with F(11) = 11 and F(f ◦ g) = F(g) ◦ F(f).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classical example: dual vector space functor V ↦ V* sending linear maps f: V→W to f* : W*→V* (reverse direction). The contravariant/co- distinction affects how compositions and induced maps behave (important in cohomology vs homology contexts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural transformation
rubrics_metrics.description: Given two functors F,G : C→D a natural transformation T from F to G assigns a morphism T_X : F(X)→G(X) to each object X ∈ C such that for each morphism f : X→Y in C the square formed by F(f), G(f), T_X, T_Y commutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The contravariant case is analogous. Examples given implicitly (e.g., boundary maps, change-of-coefficient homomorphisms) and remark that a natural transformation induces a homotopy between induced maps on classifying spaces BC→BD.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classifying space BC construction
rubrics_metrics.description: To each category C there is associated a Δ-complex BC whose n-simplices are strings X0→X1→···→Xn of morphisms in C; faces are obtained by deleting an Xi and composing adjacent morphisms if i ≠ 0,n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If C has one object with morphisms forming a group G, BC is the classifying complex BG (a K(G,1)); for a poset C(X) of simplices the classifying space BC(X) is the barycentric subdivision of X. A functor F : C→D induces a simplicial map BC→BD by applying F to each vertex simplex; a natural transformation induces a homotopy between induced maps (construction left to reader using subdivision).

rubrics_metrics.name: Homology-related functors and composition
rubrics_metrics.description: The singular chain complex functor assigns to a space X the chain complex of singular chains and to a map f : X→Y the induced chain map; the algebraic homology functor assigns to a chain complex its sequence of homology groups and to a chain map the induced homomorphisms on homology. The composition of these functors yields the singular homology functor assigning to a space its singular homology groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also described: functor assigning to a pair (X,A) the associated long exact sequence of homology groups, obtained as composition of the functor (X,A) ↦ short exact sequence of chain complexes and the functor sending such short exact sequences to long exact sequences on homology; morphisms in intermediate categories are commutative diagrams.

rubrics_metrics.name: Homology-theory axioms (wedge axiom caution)
rubrics_metrics.description: A candidate reduced homology theory may satisfy many axioms except possibly the wedge axiom: example given shows a construction where h̃_n(X) is independent of n and zero if X is finite-dimensional but wedge axiom fails.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises and remarks emphasize which axioms are necessary (e.g., suspension isomorphisms, wedge axiom) and indicate how to verify or fail them; the wedge axiom must be checked when proposing altered or reduced theories (explicitly highlighted in exercises).

rubrics_metrics.name: Homomorphism h : π1(X,x0) → H1(X) and its properties
rubrics_metrics.description: By regarding loops as singular 1-cycles there is a homomorphism h : π1(X,x0)→H1(X). If X is path-connected, h is surjective and its kernel is the commutator subgroup of π1(X), hence h induces an isomorphism from the abelianization π1(X)^{ab} onto H1(X).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses facts: constant path homologous to zero, homotopy implies homologous, product of paths corresponds to sum in homology (f g ∼ f + g), inverse path homologous to negative; combine cycles to loops at basepoint using connecting paths and reduce to a single loop; kernel analysis uses building a 2-complex from 2-simplices witnessing a 1-cycle boundary and shows resulting class lies in commutator subgroup. Example: for closed orientable surface M_g, π1(M)^{ab} ≅ Z^{2g} and basis for H1(M) given by 1-cells/loops α_i, β_i.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 2B.1 — homology of complements of embeddings
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) For an embedding h : D^k → S^n, H_i(S^n − h(D^k)) = 0 for all i. (b) For an embedding h : S^k → S^n with k < n, H_i(S^n − h(S^k)) is Z for i = n − k − 1 and 0 otherwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Special cases: Jordan curve theorem (k=1,n=2) that embedded S^1 separates S^2 into two components; complements of S^{n−1} in S^n have two components each with homology of a point. Proof technique: induction using Mayer–Vietoris decomposition of complements and compactness arguments to force cycles to be boundaries. Remarks: complements of embeddings can have nontrivial fundamental groups (Alexander horned sphere example) even when homology is the same as for the standard embedding; for embeddings of S^{n−2} in S^n the complement has homology of S^1 though π1 can vary (knot theory).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mayer–Vietoris induction technique for complements
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a decomposition A∪B of S^n minus parts of the embedded disk/sphere so that A∩B and A∪B have known homology; apply Mayer–Vietoris to relate H_i(A∪B) to H_i(A)⊕H_i(B) and induct on the dimension of embedded disk/sphere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed use in the proof of Proposition 2B.1: choose nested intervals/cubes, iterate to reduce nonboundary cycles, use compactness to derive contradictions and finish induction. Note special handling for reduced homology when i = 0.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invariance of Domain (Theorem 2B.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: If U is an open set in R^n and h : U → R^n is an embedding (or more generally a continuous injection), then the image h(U) is an open set in R^n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof passes to one-point compactifications (S^n) and reduces to showing h(D^n − ∂D^n) is open in S^n using previous proposition about complements of embeddings of spheres; consequences include: embedding of a compact n-manifold M into a connected n-manifold N must be surjective and hence a homeomorphism (Corollary 2B.4).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and finiteness constraints for division algebras over R
rubrics_metrics.description: An algebra structure on R^n is a bilinear multiplication R^n × R^n → R^n (distributive, scalar-associative). A division algebra means equations ax = b and xa = b are solvable whenever a ≠ 0, equivalently the linear maps x ↦ ax and x ↦ xa are surjective for a ≠ 0 (equivalently there are no zero-divisors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classical examples: R, C, quaternions H, octonions O. Frobenius: finite-dimensional associative division algebras with identity over R are R, C, H. Hurwitz: if multiplication preserves norms |ab| = |a||b| then dimension must be 1,2,4,8. The text proves: finite-dimensional commutative division algebra over R with identity must be R or C (dimension 1 or 2) using a topological argument: map f(x)=x^2/|x^2| on sphere induces injective quotient RP^{n−1}→S^{n−1}, forcing n=2 by homology/fundamental-group considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transfer sequence for a two-sheeted covering (Z2 coefficients)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a two-sheeted covering p: X̃ → X there is a short exact sequence of chain complexes (with Z2 coefficients) 0 → C_*(X;Z2) --τ→ C_*(X̃;Z2) --p_♯→ C_*(X;Z2) → 0, where p_♯ is surjective and τ injective (kernel of p_♯ is generated by sums of the two lifts σ1 + σ2). This yields a long exact 'transfer' sequence in homology ... → H_n(X̃;Z2) --τ_*→ H_n(X;Z2) --p_*→ H_n(X̃;Z2) → ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The map τ_* is a transfer homomorphism; the sequence is used for coverings such as p: S^n→RP^n and in computations with Z2 coefficients; naturality of the long exact sequence ensures compatibility under maps induced by odd/even maps, and is exploited to analyze degrees mod 2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Odd maps have odd degree (Proposition 2B.6) and Borsuk–Ulam consequence
rubrics_metrics.description: An odd map f : S^n → S^n (f(−x) = −f(x)) must have odd degree. Consequently, for every map g : S^n → R^n there exists x with g(x) = g(−x) (Borsuk–Ulam theorem).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses the transfer sequence for the covering S^n→RP^n with Z2 coefficients and naturality to show induced maps on the transfer sequence are isomorphisms, forcing f_* on H_n(S^n;Z2) to be an isomorphism (multiplication by degree mod 2), hence degree is odd. Borsuk–Ulam follows by building an odd map f(x) = g(x) − g(−x) and using degree considerations to force a zero.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alexander horned sphere example — complements can have wild π1 despite homology
rubrics_metrics.description: There exists an embedding S ⊂ R^3 homeomorphic to S^2 (the Alexander horned sphere) such that the unbounded component of R^3 − S is not simply-connected, even though the homology of the complement is that of a point; the construction gives an increasing union of complements whose π1 grows and whose abelianization is trivial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: nested compact subspaces X_n (balls with attached handles), complements Y_n increasing with π1(Y_n) free groups F_{2^n} embedding into the next, union has trivial abelianization because each generator is a commutator of two new generators; illustrates that homology alone does not detect knottedness, motivating study of fundamental groups and covering-space homology.
